DOC.EP: EC.02.01.01 The hospital manages safety and security risks. EP 1. The hospital identifies safety and security risks associated with the environment of care that could affect patients, staff, and other people coming to the hospital's facilities. Note: Risks are identified from internal sources such as ongoing monitoring of the environment, results of root cause analyses, results of annual proactive risk assessments of high-risk processes, and from credible external sources such as Sentinel Event Alerts. (See also

DOC.FINDING:
Safety concerns identified during the bulidng tour were very limited. The organization has done a nice job of reviewing and identifing common items on EC rounds.
In addition, a Global Risk Asssement was compelted by the safety officer.
SPECIFIC FINDINGS: During the walk-through of the facilities and specifically building nos. 1 and 22, the following safety issues were identified: 1. Oxygen storage room for CLC (Room 22-1431) contain tanks in racks. The rack with full tanks was not readily identified as "full". 2. Oxygen storage room for CLC (Room 22-1431): the door did not contain a sign stating "Caution-Oxidizing Agent Storage" "No Smoking". 3. Exhaust fan units location on the roof top were not labled "hazardous" or did not contain similar warning information to warn staff and contractor of the inherent risk of exposure to exhasut. Observed for pharmacy chemo exhaust and laboratory chemical hood exhaust systems. 4. In the old ICU (new One Day Surgery) suite, the blanket warmer indicated the temperature was above 150 degree F.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization has done a nice job of reviewing and identifing common items on EC rounds. A Global Risk Asssement was compelted by the safety officer and identified several issues for improvement. This practice should continue and include resolution of identified risks through the safety committee. Information pertaining the past SEA (Sentinel Event Alerts) such as SEA no. 48 and 47 should be addressed in the committee and by means of assessments. ? The organization should inspect all oxygen storage rooms and ensure that tank racks are labeled "empty" or "full". An appropriate sign must be place on the door stating information listed in finding no. 2. ? Roof top exhaust fan units and discharge points must be labled as "warning-hazardous exhaust" or similar warning. ? The organization must ensure that blanket warmer do not exceed maximum temperature. ECRI changed its recommendations for cabinet blanket warmers in 2009. Cabinet blanket warmers should not be set above 130º F (54ºC). Ref: ECRI Institute. ECRI Institute revises its recommendation for temperature limits on blanket warmers (hazard report). Health Devices. July 2009; 38(7): 230-231.

DOC.EP: EC.02.02.01 The hospital manages risks related to hazardous materials and waste. EP 1. The hospital maintains a written, current inventory of hazardous materials and waste that it uses, stores, or generates. The only materials that need to be included on the inventory are those whose handling, use, and storage are addressed by law and regulation. (See also IC.02.01.01, EP 6; MM.01.01.03, EP 3)
DOC.FINDING: The organization has not developed a complete and accurate list of hazardous WASTES at the facility. The list must include pharmaceuticals and chemotherapeutic drugs.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The pharmacy and safety department must review the State of Michigan hazardous medications list and determine which products they have. At a minimum, the following actions are recommended: a. The organization must review its inventory and create a current list of watses. b. “Unused Hazardous Medications” must be identified and proper disposal practices implemented. EP 3. The hospital has written procedures, including the use of precautions and personal protective equipment, to follow in response to hazardous material and waste spills or exposures.
DOC.FINDING: During review of the chemo spill plan, it was revealed that the policy did not list the required PPE (personal protective equipment) for responding to a spill. The plan did not address recommended practice and protocols for responding to spills greater than 5cc and the need for N-95 repiratory protection.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must review and update all spill plans. Appropriate PPE and proper procedure for clean-up must be listed. Staff must be fit-tested on selected respiratory protection. ? Please refer to the OSHA technical manual for control of exposures to hazardous drugs: http://www.osha.gov/dts/osta/otm/otm_vi/otm_vi_2.html EP 8. The hospital minimizes risks associated with disposing of hazardous medications. (See also MM.01.01.03, EPs 1-3)
DOC.FINDING: The organiazation is currenly in progress of implementing a plan and procedure to address this EP.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization should implement effective collection and disposl practices as soon as possible. Once the practices have been formulated, the program elements must be included in the Hazardous Materials and Waste plan. EP 12. The hospital labels hazardous materials and waste. Labels identify the contents and hazard warnings. Footnote: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s (OSHA) Bloodborne Pathogens and Hazard Communications Standards and the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) provide details on labeling requirements.
DOC.FINDING: During evaluation of EMS closets, three (3) spray bottles used for chemical cleaner dispensing were not labeled. Product information was not listed or provided for identified spray bottles.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must ensure that all hazardous materials containers are properly labeled. The label must contain the following: a. Manufacturers name b. Product name c. An appropriate hazard warning.

DOC.EP: EC.02.03.05 The hospital maintains fire safety equipment and fire safety building features. Note: This standard does not require hospitals to have the types of fire safety equipment and building features described below. However, if these types of equipment or features exist within the building, then the following maintenance, testing, and inspection requirements apply. EP 3. Every 12 months, the hospital tests duct detectors, electromechanical releasing devices, heat detectors, manual fire alarm boxes, and smoke detectors. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 72, 1999 edition (Table 7-3.2).
DOC.FINDING: For building nos. 1 and 22: Documentation provided during the review did not indicate the number of magnetic held doors tested for each building.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Test documentation must indicate the number of electromechanical doors tested during alarm activation and releasing for each building. ? PLEASE NOTE FOR ALL FIRE TEST RECORD: ? The organization must ensure that all testing records indicate the following items: 1. Name of test/activity, including number of devices tested, number passed, number failed. 2. Date completed. 3. Required frequency. 4. Name and contact information of person conducting the test. 5. NFPA standard. 6. Results or test. 7. Recommendations and follow-up if applicable. EP 4. Every 12 months, the hospital tests visual and audible fire alarms, including speakers. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 72, 1999 edition (Table 7-3.2).
DOC.FINDING: For building nos. 1 and 22: Documentation provided during the review did not indicate the number of devices tested annually for each building.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Test documentation must indicate the number of audible and visual devices tested for each building. ? PLEASE NOTE FOR ALL FIRE TEST RECORD: ? The organization must ensure that all testing records indicate the following items: 1. Name of test/activity, including number of devices tested, number passed, number failed. 2. Date completed. 3. Required frequency. 4. Name and contact information of person conducting the test. 5. NFPA standard. 6. Results or test. 7. Recommendations and follow-up if applicable. EP 12. Every 5 years, the hospital conducts water-flow tests for standpipe systems. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 25, 1998 edition.
DOC.FINDING: Review of the provided information and data indicated that this test was performed. However, pressure was not recorded and it was undetermined if the testing results were satisfactory.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must perform the 5-year water flow test and determine pressure and GPM. ? PLEASE Note: The VA has a written interpretation of understanding that this test is not reqiured if they count on the fire service to provide pressure. The organization should locate this interpretation document and determine if the test is not required. EP 13. Every 6 months, the hospital inspects any automatic fire- extinguishing systems in a kitchen. The completion dates of the inspections are documented. Note 1: Discharge of the fire-extinguishing systems is not required. Note 2: For additional guidance on performing inspections, see NFPA 96, 1998 edition.
DOC.FINDING: Over the last 12 month the hospital only completed one test. The staff was able to provide documentation for one test only.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Please have the documentation available of completed testing for every six month.

DOC.EP: EC.02.04.03 The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains medical equipment. EP 3. The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains non–life-support equipment identified on the medical equipment inventory. These activities are documented. (See also EC.02.04.01, EPs 2-4 and PC.02.01.11, EP 2)
DOC.FINDING: In the Claire CBOC, tags for two (2) pieces of medical equipment indicated that the PM (preventative maintenace) was overdue. The equipment was due for inspection in September 2011. Equipment was identified as Stimulator (sn. T1251) and a monitor (sn.1026051).
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must ensure that all equipment PM's are completed timely. ? These two items must be sent for service.

DOC.EP: EC.02.05.01 The hospital manages risks associated with its utility systems. EP 2. The hospital maintains a written inventory of all operating components of utility systems or maintains a written inventory of selected operating components of utility systems based on risks for infection, occupant needs, and systems critical to patient care (including all life-support systems). The hospital evaluates new types of utility components before initial use to determine whether they should be included in the inventory. (See also EC.02.05.05, EPs 1, 3-5)
DOC.FINDING: An inventory of utilities based on the hospitals inclusion criteria (see hospitals Environment of Care Plan-Utitilites Management) was not created. The hospital has a electronic PM and maintenance system.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must develop and maintain a complete utility inventory based on the policies inclusion criteria. ? The inventory must be available for review.

DOC.EP: EC.02.05.09 The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains medical gas and vacuum systems. Note: This standard does not require hospitals to have the medical gas and vacuum systems discussed below. However, if a hospital has these types of systems, then the following inspection, testing, and maintenance requirements apply. EP 1. In time frames defined by the hospital, the hospital inspects, tests, and maintains critical components of piped medical gas systems, including master signal panels, area alarms, automatic pressure switches, shutoff valves, flexible connectors, and outlets. These activities are documented. (See also EC.02.05.01, EP 3)
DOC.FINDING: The organization did not develop a written policy describing the components for testing, frequency of testing, and reference to manufacturer and industry approved standards for medical gas and vacuum systems.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must develop a written policy listing the elements of the medical gas system and components for testing. ? The policy must contain the organization time frames for testing listed components (zone shutoff valves, connections, outlets).

DOC.EP: EC.02.06.05 The hospital manages its environment during demolition, renovation, or new construction to reduce risk to those in the organization. EP 3. The hospital takes action based on its assessment to minimize risks during demolition, construction, or renovation.
DOC.FINDING: During review of current construction project [HVAC upgrade] in building no. 1, on floor no. 4, area FPB210- the ICRA (Infection Control Risk Assessment) calls for Class III precautions. The following was observed: 1. Negative air was provided, however indication and measurement of pressurization was not provided. 2. Sticky mats were not place at door exit. 3. Above the ceiling space was not sealed and isolated from adjacent space.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: 1. The organization ensure that industry accepted standards and the requirements for ICRA in the current FPG (Facilities Planning Guide) for construciton of healthcare facilities, 2010 are implemented. This guide has been adopted by the Joint Commission. The requirement for Class III and IV precuastions is negaitve presurization of -0.03 "H2O (inches water) or greater and direct monitoring. 2. The organization must require negative pressurization monitoring to ensure proper pressure for construction areas. 3. Stick mats must be placed at entrance in order to remove dust from workers shoes. 4. Above ceiling space must be sealed in order to provide appropriate barrier protection.

DOC.EP: EC.04.01.01 The hospital collects information to monitor conditions in the environment. EP 1. The hospital establishes a process(es) for continually monitoring, internally reporting, and investigating the following: ? Injuries to patients or others within the hospital’s facilities ? Occupational illnesses and staff injuries ? Incidents of damage to its property or the property of others ? Security incidents involving patients, staff, or others within its facilities ? Hazardous materials and waste spills and exposures ? Fire safety management problems, deficiencies, and failures ? Medical or laboratory equipment management problems, failures, and use errors ? Utility systems management problems, failures, or use errors Note 1: All the incidents and issues listed above may be reported to staff in quality assessment, improvement, or other functions. A summary of such incidents may also be shared with the person designated to coordinate safety management activities. Note 2: Review of incident reports often requires that legal processes be followed to preserve confidentiality. Opportunities to improve care, treatment, or services, or to prevent similar incidents, are not lost as a result of following the legal process.
DOC.FINDING: The organization appears to have covered most items listed this EP.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The consultant recommends that items listed in this element are clearly identified in the EC minutes and reported at least quarterly. EP 15. Every 12 months, the hospital evaluates each environment of care management plan, including a review of the plan’s objectives, scope, performance, and effectiveness. (See also EC.01.01.01, EPs 3-8;

DOC.FINDING: The hospitals annual evaluation did not effectievly list scope and objective for each plan.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must list these items in the annual evaluation for each plan and identify if the scope or objective have changed.

DOC.EP: EC.04.01.03 The hospital analyzes identified environment of care issues. EP 3. Annually, representatives from clinical, administrative, and support services recommend one or more priorities for improving the environment of care.
DOC.FINDING: The organizations EOC (Environment of Care) committee effectively collected performance data. However, discussion of PI measure data and selection of a “measure for improvement” by the leadership was not completed.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organizations EOC committee must seek approval of one or more measures at least annually. The committee must send these specific measures based on the committees selection of priorities identified during EOC activities. Documentation of selection and acceptance by the leadership must be documented at least annually, preferably during the annual review process. ? Routine (quarterly) progress of selected PI measure must be reported and monitored.
